sections.h2: Can living in a house make someone the owner?
sections.html:
Only if they meet every element of the adverse possession statute for ten years, including a written document that looks like a title and payment of the property taxes. Section 37-1-22 NMSA 1978 controls. Someone who moves into a vacant house with no paper claim and never pays the tax bill is nowhere close.

The statute requires adverse possession "continuously and in good faith under color of title for ten years," with no lawsuit brought by the true owner in that time. Once those conditions are met, the occupant may keep the land described in the writing that gives color of title, and an owner who sat on a claim for the ten years is barred. Adverse possession is defined as "an actual and visible appropriation of land, commenced and continued under a color of title and claim of right inconsistent with and hostile to the claim of another."

A separate tax condition closes the statute. Adverse possession isn't established unless the claimant, or those the claimant takes through, continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed against the property during the ten years.

Legal aid guidance prepared for the state's Land Grant Council groups the requirements in three parts: open, continuous, exclusive, actual, visible, hostile and notorious possession for ten years, color of title, and payment of taxes. Every one must hold for the full ten years, and failing any one defeats the claim.

  • Continuous: possession can't be on and off.
  • Actual: the claimant must physically enter. Holding a deed isn't enough, because the ten years don't begin until the claimant enters and takes possession.
  • Open and notorious: the claimant can't hide. The clock doesn't run until the possession is visible enough to give the owner notice.
  • Exclusive: possession can't be shared with the public or other users. If others try to use the land, the claimant has to keep them out.
  • Hostile: the occupant must be there without any right or permission, so the possession is plainly against the owner's rights.
Requirements at a glance
RequirementWhat the claimant needs
TimeTen years, with no suit by the owner
Written claimColor of title, held in good faith
TaxesAll state, county and municipal taxes paid continuously
ProofClear and convincing evidence

The claimant carries the burden. Adverse possession must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and it can't be established by inference or implication.

Color of title is a written document that purports to give the occupant title, even if it turns out to be defective. New Mexico courts have accepted quitclaim deeds, a certificate of sale for taxes, a government patent, a void deed, and a quiet title decree or other court judgment.

Case notes under 37-1-22 add detail. A recorded quitclaim deed, executed and acknowledged one day and recorded the next, with the buyer taking immediate possession, established color of title in one case. A tax deed can serve even when void for lack of title in the grantor, but not if its land description is too weak to identify the property. In one case involving siblings who owned together, a deed to one sibling and his wife did not establish color of title.

A stray deed in the record can matter. If someone lives in your house and has recorded a deed, even a weak one, the ten-year clock may have started. Our New Mexico quitclaim deed guide explains the form that often shows up in these disputes.

Almost never, because permission defeats hostility. Where the original entry was permissive, the statute of limitations doesn't begin to run until an adverse holding is declared and notice of the change reaches the owner. Mere possession isn't enough. Possession that starts as a tenancy is presumed permissive, and ending that presumption takes proof, or a presumption, that the owner was told the occupant now claims against them.

Someone who enters a vacant house without permission is in a different position, but the extra requirements still apply. Claimants have won by marking boundaries, posting no-trespassing signs, clearing land, fencing, limiting access and paying taxes. Together, those facts gave the owner notice. Simply staying in a house with none of those steps is thin evidence.

The statute also protects some owners with a disability. If the person entitled to sue was imprisoned, of unsound mind or under the age of majority when the cause of action first accrued, they get one year after the disability ends to bring suit. Cumulative disabilities don't extend the bar.

sections.h2: Government land, water rights and land grants
sections.html:
Not every kind of property can be taken this way. Adverse possession usually can't be applied against governmental property, only private property. Land grants governed as political subdivisions were made immune from adverse possession claims in 2007 under 49-1-11.2, except for claims that had already vested by June 15, 2007.

Two more limits apply. New Mexico's water code means water rights can't be obtained through adverse possession, and the state's rights in highways can't be divested by it under a cross-referenced statute.

sections.h2: How an owner removes someone with no right to be there
sections.html:
Through a court case. A landlord must go to court before evicting a tenant, and a person living in a home who isn't on the lease can't be evicted like a tenant. That person is removed through "forcible entry," using Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. At the hearing, the judge decides whether the person must leave and how much time they have to move out.

Section 35-10-1 NMSA 1978 lists the grounds for a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action in magistrate court. The first applies directly to uninvited occupants: the defendant entered and occupied the land of another against the owner's will or consent and refused to vacate after notice from the owner, agent or attorney. The other grounds cover:

  • A tenant who holds over after the lease ends or contrary to its terms.
  • A tenant who fails to pay rent when due.
  • An occupant who stays after a mortgage foreclosure or execution sale, unless claiming title paramount to the mortgage or derived from the purchaser.
  • A month-to-month tenant or tenant at will who stays after thirty days' written notice to vacate.

The district court has concurrent jurisdiction when the rent or reasonable rental value is $50 or more per month. These actions are summary proceedings that settle nothing about title. A forcible entry case puts the parties back in their prior positions but doesn't decide who owns the house.

Section 30-14-1.1 NMSA 1978 makes several kinds of trespass a misdemeanor. One is entering and remaining on another's land after being asked to leave. Others are entering land posted against trespass at every roadway or apparent way of access, and driving a vehicle onto fenced land except through an apparent way of access.

The same section creates civil liability. A person who enters another's land without permission and damages the realty or its improvements, including buildings, structures, trees and shrubs, owes double the appraised value of the damage to the owner, lessee or person in lawful possession.

The offense turns on a request to leave, so keep a dated written request. Talk to an attorney before acting.

sections.h2: Protecting a vacant or inherited house
sections.html:
Keep the paper record clean and the taxes current. These steps follow from the statute:

  • Visit the property on a schedule, and document each visit with dates and photos.
  • Post no-trespassing signs and keep the property secured.
  • Pay the property tax yourself. A claimant who hasn't paid can't succeed, and a delinquency can lead to a tax sale, covered in our New Mexico tax deed guide.
  • Check the county clerk's records for any deed or affidavit recorded by someone else.
  • Give written notice to anyone staying without permission, and keep a copy.

Under a 1954 decision, the general rule is that continuity of adverse possession is interrupted if the land is forfeited to the state for taxes. That is one more reason to keep the tax record current.

Owners who inherited a house and can't manage an occupant, repairs or back taxes sometimes sell as is. Cash Home Buyers doesn't promise a price in advance. Anyone who buys will want to know who lives in the house and whether a court case is pending, so share that up front.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in New Mexico?
faqs.a: Ten years of continuous possession under color of title, in good faith, with all taxes paid, under 37-1-22 NMSA 1978. The claimant must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights in New Mexico?
faqs.a: A person with no written claim to title who hasn't paid the property taxes can't meet the statute. The owner removes an occupant through a forcible entry complaint in court.

faqs.q: Do adverse possession claimants have to pay property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Adverse possession isn't established unless the claimant or predecessors continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed during the ten years.

faqs.q: How do I remove someone who is not on the lease?
faqs.a: File Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. The judge decides whether the person must leave and sets the time to move out.

faqs.q: Is it a crime to stay on someone's land after being told to leave?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 30-14-1.1 makes it a misdemeanor to enter and remain on another's land after being asked to leave. A forcible entry case, by contrast, doesn't decide title, so a separate action is needed to settle ownership.
